title: STAT 579: Applied Causal Inference
text:
Course Overview
This graduate seminar offers a practical and intuitive journey into modern causal inference methods. We will explore how to move beyond simple correlation to identify and estimate causal effects from both experimental and observational data, with a focus on applications in public health, epidemiology, and clinical research.
The course emphasizes a rigorous, assumption-driven approach. A central component is a semester-long research project where you will frame an observational study as a target trial emulation, applying modern methods to answer a causal question with real-world data.

Key Topics You Will Master:

The Potential Outcomes Framework & SUTVA
Causal Graphs (DAGs) for Assumption Transparency
Confounding and Selection Bias Identification
Propensity Scores (Matching & Weighting)
Marginal Structural Models for Time-Varying Treatments
Instrumental Variables (IV)
Causal Mediation Analysis (NDE/NIE)
Sensitivity Analysis for Unmeasured Confounding

title: Interpreting Potential Outcomes Across Causal Inference Methods
text: The potential outcomes framework provides a unified mathematical language for causal inference, but the same notation can carry dramatically different interpretations depending on the identification strategy employed. Understanding these contextual differences is crucial for proper application and interpretation of causal methods. This chapter explores how potential outcome notation adapts across mediation analysis, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, and time-varying interventions, revealing both the flexibility and precision required in modern causal reasoning.

title: Interpreting Potential Outcomes Across Causal Inference Methods
text: The potential outcomes framework provides a unified mathematical language for causal inference, but the same notation can carry dramatically different interpretations depending on the identification strategy employed. Understanding these contextual differences is crucial for proper application and interpretation of causal methods. This chapter explores how potential outcome notation adapts across mediation analysis, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, and time-varying interventions, revealing both the flexibility and precision required in modern causal reasoning.

title: Interpreting Potential Outcomes Across Causal Inference Methods
text:
1. Mediation Analysis: Cross-World Counterfactuals

The Challenge of Nested Potential Outcomes
In mediation analysis, we encounter the most complex form of potential outcome notation: nested counterfactuals of the form \(Y^{a, M^{a'}}\). This notation describes outcomes in hypothetical worlds that combine elements from multiple parallel universes.

Deconstructing the Superscript: \(Y^{a, M^{a'}}\)
The superscript contains two conceptually distinct components:
Component 1: Direct Intervention (\(a\))

Represents an active manipulation of treatment \(A\) to value \(a\)
This is a standard intervention, similar to what we see in randomized experiments

Component 2: Counterfactual Mediator Value (\(M^{a'}\))

This is not an intervention on \(M\)
Instead, \(M^{a'}\) represents the natural value that mediator \(M\) would have taken if treatment had been set to \(a'\)
Crucially, \(M^{a'}\) is a random variable capturing natural variation in mediator response



The Cross-World Interpretation
\(Y^{a, M^{a'}}\) means: “The potential outcome that would be realized if we intervened to set treatment \(A\) to \(a\), while the mediator \(M\) simultaneously took on the value it would have naturally attained if treatment had been set to \(a'\).”
This creates a “cross-world” counterfactual requiring information from multiple parallel universes:

World 1: Where \(A = a'\) (to determine \(M^{a'}\))
World 2: Where \(A = a\) and \(M = M^{a'}\) (to determine \(Y\))



Natural Direct and Indirect Effects
Natural Direct Effect (NDE)
\[
\text{NDE} = \E{Y^{a=1, M^{a=0}} - Y^{a=0, M^{a=0}}}
\]
Interpretation: Compare two worlds where the mediator is frozen at its natural control value (\(M^{a=0}\)). Only the treatment varies. Any difference isolates the pathway that bypasses the mediator.
Natural Indirect Effect (NIE)
\[
\text{NIE} = \E{Y^{a=1, M^{a=1}} - Y^{a=1, M^{a=0}}}
\]
Interpretation: Treatment is fixed at the treated level. Only the mediator’s natural value changes (from control to treatment level). Any difference isolates the pathway flowing through the mediator.


Alternative Mediation Frameworks
Controlled Direct Effects
\[
\text{CDE}(m) = \E{Y^{a=1, m} - Y^{a=0, m}}
\]
Here, the mediator is set to a fixed value \(m\) (not a counterfactual value). This represents a different causal question: the effect of treatment when we directly control the mediator.
Interventional Effects (Vanderweele & Tchetgen Tchetgen) These effects consider interventions that shift the distribution of the mediator rather than fixing it to specific values, providing yet another interpretation of “mediated” effects.

title: Interpreting Potential Outcomes Across Causal Inference Methods
text:
2. Instrumental Variables: Compliance-Defined Counterfactuals

The Instrumental Variable Setup
In IV analysis, potential outcomes take on a different meaning, intimately connected to the concept of compliance types. The notation \(Y^z\) represents the outcome that would be observed if the instrument \(Z\) were set to \(z\), but this masks considerable heterogeneity.

Compliance Types and Potential Outcomes
Consider instrument \(Z \in \{0,1\}\) and treatment \(A \in \{0,1\}\). Each unit has potential treatment values \((A^0, A^1)\), defining four compliance types:

Always-takers: \(A^0 = 1, A^1 = 1\)
Never-takers: \(A^0 = 0, A^1 = 0\)
Compliers: \(A^0 = 0, A^1 = 1\)
Defiers: \(A^0 = 1, A^1 = 0\)



The Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE)
The IV estimand identifies the Local Average Treatment Effect:
\[
\text{LATE} = \E{Y^1 - Y^0 | \text{Complier}}
\]
Critical Interpretation: \(Y^1\) and \(Y^0\) here do not represent potential outcomes under direct intervention on \(Y\). Instead:

\(Y^1\) = outcome when instrument encourages treatment (and compliers take treatment)
\(Y^0\) = outcome when instrument discourages treatment (and compliers avoid treatment)



The Indirect Nature of IV Counterfactuals
Unlike in experimental settings, IV counterfactuals are mediated through compliance behavior:
\[
Y^z = \sum_{\text{types}} Y^{A^z} \cdot \ind{\text{type}} \cdot \Prob{\text{type}}
\]
This shows that \(Y^z\) is actually a mixture of different potential outcomes, weighted by compliance type probabilities.


Principal Stratification Framework
In IV analysis, we’re essentially doing principal stratification on compliance types:

Principal strata: Defined by \((A^0, A^1)\)
Causal effect of interest: \(\E{Y^{A=1} - Y^{A=0} | A^0 = 0, A^1 = 1}\)
Identification: Uses the instrument to reveal this stratum-specific effect



Exclusion Restriction Interpretation
The exclusion restriction (\(Y^{z,d} = Y^d\) for all \(z,d\)) means:
“The instrument only affects outcomes through its effect on treatment receipt.”
This creates a specific type of mediation structure where the instrument → treatment → outcome, but unlike general mediation, we can point-identify the effect for compliers under additional assumptions.

title: Interpreting Potential Outcomes Across Causal Inference Methods
text:
3. Difference-in-Differences: Temporal Counterfactuals

The DiD Framework
In difference-in-differences, potential outcomes acquire a temporal dimension. The notation \(Y_{it}^g\) represents the outcome for unit \(i\) at time \(t\) if first treated in period \(g\).

Treatment Timing and Potential Outcomes
Never-treated units: \(Y_{it}^{\infty}\) (outcome if never treated) Treated units: \(Y_{it}^g\) where \(g\) is the first treatment period


Parallel Trends as a Counterfactual Assumption
The parallel trends assumption states:
\[
\E{Y_{it}^{\infty} - Y_{i,t-1}^{\infty} | G_i = g} = \E{Y_{it}^{\infty} - Y_{i,t-1}^{\infty} | G_i = \infty}
\]
Interpretation: The counterfactual trend for treated units (had they not been treated) equals the observed trend for control units.


The ATT in DiD
The Average Treatment Effect on the Treated becomes:
\[
\text{ATT}_{g,t} = \E{Y_{it}^g - Y_{it}^{\infty} | G_i = g, t \geq g}
\]
Key insight: We observe \(Y_{it}^g\) but must construct \(Y_{it}^{\infty}\) using the parallel trends assumption and control group observations.


Staggered Adoption and Dynamic Effects
Modern DiD with staggered treatment timing:
\[
Y_{it}^g = Y_{it}^{\infty} + \sum_{s=0}^{\infty} \tau_{g,s} \cdot \mathbf{1}{t = g + s}
\]
where \(\tau_{g,s}\) is the treatment effect \(s\) periods after initial treatment for cohort \(g\).
Interpretation complexity: Each potential outcome \(Y_{it}^g\) now represents a dynamic treatment trajectory starting at time \(g\), not just a static treatment state.

title: Interpreting Potential Outcomes Across Causal Inference Methods
text:
4. Time-Varying Interventions: Sequential Counterfactuals

The g-Formula Framework
For time-varying treatments \(\bar{A}_t = (A_0, A_1, \ldots, A_t)\), potential outcomes become path-dependent: \(Y^{\bar{a}_t}\).

Sequential Randomization
The key assumption becomes sequential exchangeability:
\[
Y^{\bar{a}_t} \indep A_t | \bar{A}_{t-1} = \bar{a}_{t-1}, \bar{L}_t
\]
Interpretation: At each time point, treatment assignment is as-good-as-random given observed history.


The g-Formula
\[
\E{Y^{\bar{a}_t}} = \sum_{\bar{l}_t} \E{Y | \bar{A}_t = \bar{a}_t, \bar{L}_t = \bar{l}_t} \prod_{k=0}^t \Prob{L_k = l_k | \bar{A}_{k-1} = \bar{a}_{k-1}, \bar{L}_{k-1} = \bar{l}_{k-1}}
\]
Interpretation: The counterfactual mean under treatment regime \(\bar{a}_t\) equals a weighted average over all possible covariate histories, where weights represent the probability of each history under the treatment regime.


Sustained vs. Point Interventions
Sustained intervention: \(\bar{a}_t = (1,1,\ldots,1)\) - “always treat” Point intervention: \(\bar{a}_t = (0,\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots,0)\) - “treat only at time \(s\)”
Each creates different counterfactual worlds with distinct causal interpretations.


Natural vs. Modified Treatment Policies
Static regimes: \(\bar{a}_t\) fixed regardless of evolving covariates Dynamic regimes: \(a_t = d_t(\bar{l}_t)\) where treatment depends on covariate history Modified treatment policies: Shift observed treatment probabilities rather than imposing fixed regimes

title: Interpreting Potential Outcomes Across Causal Inference Methods
section: 5. Comparative Analysis: How Context Shapes Interpretation
text:
5. Comparative Analysis: How Context Shapes Interpretation

Common Mathematical Forms, Different Meanings









Method
Notation
Core Interpretation
Key Challenge




RCT
\(Y^a\)
Outcome under direct intervention
Simple, unconfounded


Mediation
\(Y^{a, M^{a'}}\)
Cross-world counterfactual
Requires multiple universes


IV
\(Y^z\)
Outcome under instrument-induced treatment
Compliance heterogeneity


DiD
\(Y_{it}^g\)
Outcome under treatment starting at time \(g\)
Parallel trends assumption


Time-varying
\(Y^{\bar{a}_t}\)
Outcome under treatment sequence
Sequential confounding





Identification Strategies and Assumptions
Mediation Analysis

Sequential ignorability: \((Y^{a,m}, M^{a'}) \indep A | X\) and \(Y^{a,m} \indep M | A, X\)
Cross-world independence: Cannot be tested empirically

Instrumental Variables

Instrument relevance: \(\cov{Z, A} \neq 0\)
Exclusion restriction: \(Y^{z,d} = Y^d\)
Monotonicity: No defiers

Difference-in-Differences

Parallel trends: \(\E{Y_{it}^{\infty} - Y_{i,t-1}^{\infty} | G_i = g} = \E{Y_{it}^{\infty} - Y_{i,t-1}^{\infty} | G_i = \infty}\)
No anticipation: Treatment doesn’t affect outcomes before implementation

Time-Varying Interventions

Sequential exchangeability: \(Y^{\bar{a}_t} \indep A_t | \bar{A}_{t-1} = \bar{a}_{t-1}, \bar{L}_t\)
Positivity: \(P(A_t = a_t | \bar{A}_{t-1} = \bar{a}_{t-1}, \bar{L}_t = \bar{l}_t) > 0\)



The Role of Time in Counterfactual Reasoning
Static potential outcomes (RCT, basic mediation): Time-invariant treatment effects Dynamic potential outcomes (DiD): Treatment effects can vary with exposure duration Sequential potential outcomes (Time-varying): Treatment history determines outcomes

title: Interpreting Potential Outcomes Across Causal Inference Methods
text:
6. Advanced Topics and Extensions

Interference and Spillover Effects
When units interfere with each other, potential outcomes become:
\[
Y_i^{\bar{a}_N} = Y_i(a_i, a_{-i})
\]
where \(a_{-i}\) represents treatment assignments for all other units. This creates network-dependent counterfactuals.


Mediation with Time-Varying Treatments
Combining mediation and time-varying interventions:
\[
Y^{\bar{a}_t, \bar{M}^{\bar{a}'_t}}
\]
Interpretation: Outcome under treatment sequence \(\bar{a}_t\) with mediator trajectory that would have emerged under alternative sequence \(\bar{a}'_t\).


Survival Analysis and Truncation by Death
In survival settings:
\[
Y^a = Y(a) \text{ if } T(a) > t, \text{ undefined otherwise}
\]
Interpretation: Potential outcomes may not be well-defined if treatment affects survival. This leads to principal stratification on survival status.


Machine Learning and Potential Outcomes
Modern methods (double/debiased ML) estimate:
\[
\E{Y^1 - Y^0} = \E{\E{Y|A=1,X} - \E{Y|A=0,X}}
\]
Interpretation: The same potential outcome difference, but estimated via outcome regression functions rather than direct randomization.

title: Interpreting Potential Outcomes Across Causal Inference Methods
text:
7. Practical Guidelines for Interpretation

Checklist for Interpreting Potential Outcomes

Identify the intervention type

Direct manipulation vs. instrument-induced vs. natural variation

Understand the reference population

Entire population vs. compliers vs. treated units vs. survivors

Consider temporal aspects

Static vs. dynamic vs. sequential treatments

Examine cross-world dependencies

Single universe vs. multiple counterfactual worlds

Assess identification assumptions

What makes the counterfactual identifiable from observed data?




Common Misinterpretations
Mediation Analysis

Error: Treating \(M^{a'}\) as an intervention rather than counterfactual value
Correction: Recognize that mediation effects require cross-world reasoning

Instrumental Variables

Error: Interpreting LATE as population average treatment effect
Correction: Remember LATE applies only to compliers

Difference-in-Differences

Error: Assuming treatment effects are constant over time
Correction: Allow for dynamic treatment effects and test parallel trends

Time-Varying Interventions

Error: Ignoring time-varying confounding
Correction: Use g-formula or marginal structural models

title: Interpreting Potential Outcomes Across Causal Inference Methods
section: Conclusion: The Art of Causal Interpretation
text:
Conclusion: The Art of Causal Interpretation
The potential outcomes framework provides remarkable flexibility for expressing diverse causal questions, but this flexibility comes with the responsibility of careful interpretation. The same mathematical notation can represent fundamentally different causal concepts depending on the identification strategy employed.
Understanding these distinctions is not merely academic—it directly impacts:

Study design decisions: What assumptions are reasonable for your setting?
Estimation strategies: Which methods are appropriate for your causal question?
Policy interpretation: What populations and scenarios do your results apply to?

The evolution of causal inference continues to expand our ability to answer complex causal questions, but the fundamental requirement remains unchanged: precise thinking about counterfactual scenarios and the assumptions that make them identifiable from observed data.
As the field advances toward more complex settings—network interference, continuous treatments, high-dimensional mediators, machine learning integration—the principles outlined in this chapter provide the foundation for rigorous causal reasoning. The mathematics may grow more sophisticated, but the core interpretive challenges remain: What counterfactual world are we imagining, and what assumptions allow us to learn about it from the world we observe?

title: Week 2: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
Week 2: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
Week 2: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
text:
1. Chains (Mediation): \(A \rightarrow M \leftarrow Y\)
This structure represents a causal pathway where the effect of an exposure (\(A\)) on an outcome (\(Y\)) is transmitted through a mediating variable (\(M\)).

Example 1: A smoking cessation program (\(A\)) causes an individual to reduce their cigarette consumption (\(M\)), which in turn reduces their risk of lung cancer (\(Y\)).
Example 2: A new drug (\(A\)) improves a patient’s cholesterol levels (\(M\)), which in turn lowers their risk of a heart attack (\(Y\)).
Statistical Property: \(A\) and \(Y\) are associated. If we condition on the mediator \(M\), we block this causal path, and the statistical association between \(A\) and \(Y\) will weaken or disappear.

title: Week 2: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
text:
2. Forks (Confounding): \(A \leftarrow C \rightarrow Y\)
This is the classic structure of confounding. A variable \(C\) is a common cause of both the exposure (\(A\)) and the outcome (\(Y\)).

Example 1: An individual’s socioeconomic status (\(C\)) may affect their choice of neighborhood (and thus exposure to air pollution, \(A\)) as well as their underlying health (and thus risk of asthma, \(Y\)).
Example 2: A patient’s baseline disease severity (\(C\)) might influence a doctor’s decision to prescribe an aggressive new treatment (\(A\)) and also directly affect the patient’s survival (\(Y\)).
Statistical Property: \(A\) and \(Y\) are associated due to the common cause \(C\). To estimate the true causal effect of \(A\) on \(Y\), we must condition on the confounder \(C\).

title: Week 2: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
text:
3. Colliders: A → C ← Y
This structure occurs when an exposure (\(A\)) and an outcome (\(Y\)) are independent causes of a third variable, \(C\). Because the arrows “collide” at \(C\), it is called a collider.

Example 1: Admission to a specialized hospital unit (\(C\)) is caused by having a rare disease (\(A\)) or having severe symptoms from an unrelated condition (\(Y\)).
Example 2: A patient’s self-reported “wellness score” (\(C\)) is high if they have either good physical health (\(A\)) or good mental health (\(Y\)).
Statistical Property: \(A\) and \(Y\) are marginally independent. Conditioning on a collider \(C\) opens a non-causal path and induces a spurious association between \(A\) and \(Y\).







Pitfall: Conditioning on a Collider



Controlling for a collider is a common and serious mistake in applied research. It often occurs through sample selection. For instance, studying the effect of a risk factor (\(A\)) on a disease (\(Y\)) using only hospitalized patients (\(C\)) can induce collider bias if both \(A\) and \(Y\) lead to hospitalization.
The rule is simple: Do not condition on colliders.

title: Week 2: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
text:
Check Your Understanding
For each scenario, identify the structure (Chain, Fork, or Collider) and state whether you should condition on the middle variable (\(Z\)).

Scenario A: \(A\) (Diet Soda Intake) → \(Z\) (Desire for Sweets) → \(Y\) (Weight Gain). Should you condition on \(Z\) to find the total effect of diet soda on weight gain?
Scenario B: \(A\) (Genetics for high cholesterol) ← \(Z\) (Shared Family Environment) → \(Y\) (Dietary Habits). Should you condition on \(Z\) to find the effect of genetics on diet?
Scenario C: \(A\) (Patient has Condition X) → \(Z\) (Is selected for a clinical trial) ← \(Y\) (Patient lives near the research hospital). Should you condition on \(Z\) to find the effect of Condition X on where a patient lives?



Answer


Chain (Mediation). No, you should not condition on \(Z\) if you want the total causal effect of \(A\) on \(Y\). Conditioning on a mediator blocks the causal pathway.
Fork (Confounding). Yes, you must condition on \(Z\). \(Z\) is a common cause of \(A\) and \(Y\) and creates a spurious association.
Collider. No, absolutely not. \(Z\) is a collider. Conditioning on it would create a spurious association between the patient’s condition and their location.

title: Week 2: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
section: 📕 Motivation: The Theory Connecting DAGs to Data
text:
📕 Motivation: The Theory Connecting DAGs to Data
Why can we trust the graphical rules of d-separation? The connection between a DAG’s structure and the statistical properties of the data it represents is formalized by two key assumptions: the Causal Markov Assumption and the Faithfulness Assumption. Together, they allow us to read conditional independencies directly from the graph.

Causal Markov Assumption: This assumption states that, conditional on its direct causes (its “parents” in the DAG), a variable is independent of all its non-descendants. This is the formal basis for why controlling for confounders works.
Faithfulness Assumption: This assumption states that all conditional independencies present in the data are represented in the DAG. In other words, there are no “accidental” cancellations of effects that would create an independence where the graph suggests a dependence. For example, if a drug has a positive direct effect on health but also a negative indirect effect (via a side effect) that perfectly cancels out the positive effect, the data would show no association. This would be a violation of faithfulness.

title: Week 2: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
section: 📕 Derivation: How d-Separation Implies Conditional Independence
text:
📕 Derivation: How d-Separation Implies Conditional Independence
Let’s use our confounding example (A ← Z → Y) to provide a conceptual derivation of why conditioning on \(Z\) makes \(A\) and \(Y\) independent (if there is no direct arrow between them).

Start with the Joint Probability Distribution: According to the rules of probability and the Causal Markov assumption, we can factorize the joint distribution P(A, Z, Y) based on the DAG’s structure. Each variable’s probability is conditioned only on its parents: \[
P(A, Z, Y) = P(Z) \times P(A|Z) \times P(Y|Z)
\]

Annotation: \(Z\) has no parents, so its probability is marginal. \(A\)’s only parent is \(Z\), so we have P(A|Z). \(Y\)’s only parent is \(Z\), so we have P(Y|Z).

Derive the Conditional Distribution of A and Y given Z: We want to know P(A, Y | Z). Using the definition of conditional probability: \[P(A, Y | Z) = \frac{P(A, Y, Z)}{P(Z)}\]
Substitute the Factorized Form: Now, substitute our factorization from Step 1 into the numerator: \[
P(A, Y | Z) = \frac{P(Z) \times P(A|Z) \times P(Y|Z)}{P(Z)}
\]
Simplify: The P(Z) terms cancel out, leaving: \[
P(A, Y | Z) = P(A|Z) \times P(Y|Z)
\]
Conclusion: This final expression is the definition of conditional independence. It shows that, given \(Z\), the joint probability of \(A\) and \(Y\) is just the product of their individual conditional probabilities. Therefore, \(A\) is independent of \(Y\) conditional on \(Z\), written as (A ⊥ Y | Z).

This derivation demonstrates that the graphical rule of “blocking” a backdoor path by conditioning on the common cause \(Z\) is mathematically equivalent to achieving conditional independence in the data. This is the theoretical foundation that allows us to use DAGs to design valid statistical analyses for causal inference.

section: Part 1: The Language of Causality (Tuesday Session)
text:
Part 1: The Language of Causality (Tuesday Session)

The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference
The central challenge of causal inference can be stated simply: we can never observe an individual’s outcome under both treatment and control at the same time. For any person, we see what happened, but we can never see what would have happened under a different choice. This unobservable outcome is known as the counterfactual.
Causal inference, therefore, is a scientific approach to dealing with a missing data problem. For every individual, at least one potential outcome is missing.


🧠 Clarifying The Concept: The Two Paths Analogy

Imagine you are a doctor with a patient who has high blood pressure. You stand at a fork in the road for their treatment plan. Path A is to prescribe a new drug. Path B is to prescribe a placebo. You can only choose one path. If you choose the drug (Path A), you will observe their blood pressure in a month. But you will never know what their blood pressure would have been had you chosen the placebo (Path B) at that same moment. That un-chosen path represents the counterfactual. The core task of causal inference is to find rigorous ways to compare the destinations of Path A and Path B, even though no single patient can ever travel both.



The Potential Outcomes Framework
To reason about these two paths, we use the Potential Outcomes framework (also called the Neyman-Rubin Causal Model). Let’s establish our notation for a simple scenario with a binary treatment.

Unit \(i\): An individual in our study (e.g., a patient, a person, a school).
Treatment \(Z_i\): A binary variable, where \(Z_i=1\) if unit \(i\) receives the treatment and \(Z_i=0\) if unit \(i\) receives the control.
Potential Outcomes \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\): These are the pre-existing, latent outcomes for unit \(i\) under both possible scenarios.

\(Y_i(1)\): The outcome for unit \(i\) if they were to receive the treatment (\(Z=1\)).
\(Y_i(0)\): The outcome for unit \(i\) if they were to receive the control (\(Z=0\)).


For any given individual, both \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\) are assumed to exist before any treatment is actually assigned.


The Individual Causal Effect (\(\tau_i\))
The individual causal effect (\(\tau_i\), or “tau”) is the difference between these two potential outcomes for a single unit:
\[
\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)
\]
Because of the Fundamental Problem, we can never observe \(\tau_i\) for any individual. We can only observe one of the two potential outcomes. The observed outcome, \(Y_i\), is linked to the potential outcomes through the treatment assignment \(Z_i\):
\[
Y_i = Z_i \cdot Y_i(1) + (1-Z_i) \cdot Y_i(0)
\]
This is a compact way to say that if \(Z_i=1\), we observe \(Y_i(1)\); if \(Z_i=0\), we observe \(Y_i(0)\).

Let’s test a new blood pressure drug on 6 patients. Imagine we have a “God’s-eye view” and can see all potential outcomes (in mmHg).

From this complete data, we can see the true causal effect for each person. But in reality, we can’t see this full table.


From Individuals to Populations: The Average Treatment Effect (ATE)
Since we cannot access \(\tau_i\), we shift our goal to a more feasible target: the Average Treatment Effect (ATE). The ATE is the average of the individual causal effects across our population of interest.
\[
\text{ATE} = E[\tau_i] = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]
\]
By the linearity of expectation, a fundamental rule in probability, we can rewrite this as:
\[
\text{ATE} = E[Y_i(1)] - E[Y_i(0)]
\]
Using our “God’s-eye view” data, the true ATE is:

\(E[Y(1)] = (130 + 125 + 140 + 135 + 150 + 140) / 6 = 136.67\)
\(E[Y(0)] = (145 + 130 + 150 + 155 + 155 + 145) / 6 = 146.67\)
True ATE = \(136.67 - 146.67 = \mathbf{-10.0}\) mmHg



📌 Key Assumption: SUTVA
The entire Potential Outcomes framework rests on the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA). This is a crucial assumption we make in almost all causal analyses. SUTVA has two parts:

No Interference: The potential outcomes for one unit are unaffected by the treatment assignment of other units.

Public Health Example: In a vaccine trial, if vaccinating person A reduces the chance that person B (in the placebo group) gets the flu, then person B’s outcome has been “interfered” with by person A’s treatment. This violates the no-interference assumption. These are often called “spillover” effects.

Consistency (or “One Version of Treatment”): For a unit \(i\) who received treatment \(Z_i=z\), their observed outcome \(Y_i\) is equal to their potential outcome \(Y_i(z)\). This implies that there is only one “version” of the treatment.

Public Health Example: A therapy program is the “treatment.” If some therapists are far more effective than others, then a patient’s outcome depends not just on getting therapy (\(Z=1\)), but on which therapist they got. In this case, there are multiple versions of the treatment, and the consistency assumption may be violated.

Selection Bias: The Arch-Nemesis of Causal Inference
The simplest way to estimate the effect is to compare the average outcomes in the two groups. But is this comparison valid? Let’s decompose the “naïve” difference in means:
\[
\underbrace{E[Y | Z=1] - E[Y | Z=0]}_{\text{Naïve Difference}} = \underbrace{E[Y(1) | Z=1] - E[Y(0) | Z=0]}_{\text{What we can calculate}}
\]
Through a small algebraic trick (see Appendix), we can rewrite this as:
\[
\text{Naïve Difference} = \underbrace{E[Y(1) - Y(0) | Z=1]}_{\text{ATT}} + \underbrace{\{E[Y(0) | Z=1] - E[Y(0) | Z=0]\}}_{\text{Selection Bias}}
\]
where ATT is the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated.






Selection Bias



Selection Bias is the systematic difference in baseline potential outcomes (\(Y(0)\)) between the group that receives treatment and the group that does not. In observational studies, this is almost always present. For example, sicker patients may be more likely to seek out a new treatment, meaning the treated group was less healthy to begin with. This bias will distort our estimate of the causal effect.




Randomization To the Rescue
This is where the magic of the Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) comes in. By randomly assigning the treatment \(Z\), we sever any systematic link between the treatment and the potential outcomes. On average, the group that gets the treatment is identical to the group that gets the control on all baseline characteristics, both observed and unobserved.






Theorem: Independence by Randomization



In an ideal RCT, the treatment assignment \(Z\) is statistically independent of the potential outcomes \((Y(1), Y(0))\). We write this as:
\[
(Y(1), Y(0)) \perp Z
\]
This implies that the expectation of a potential outcome is the same regardless of which group you look at:

\(E[Y(0) | Z=1] = E[Y(0) | Z=0] = E[Y(0)]\)
\(E[Y(1) | Z=1] = E[Y(1) | Z=0] = E[Y(1)]\)



Because of this property, the selection bias term becomes zero:
\[
\text{Selection Bias} = E[Y(0) | Z=1] - E[Y(0) | Z=0] = 0
\]
And our decomposition simplifies beautifully:
\[
E[Y | Z=1] - E[Y | Z=0] = E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)] = \text{ATE}
\]
This proves that in an RCT, the simple difference in observed means is an unbiased estimator of the Average Treatment Effect.


Estimation And Lab Preview
Our estimator for the ATE, denoted \(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}\), is the sample difference-in-means:
\[
\hat{\tau}_{ATE} = \bar{Y}_{Z=1} - \bar{Y}_{Z=0}
\]
✅ Example: Estimating the ATE from Observed Data
Using our observed data:

Treated Group (\(Z=1\)): {130, 140, 150}. Mean \(\bar{Y}_1 = 140.0\).
Control Group (\(Z=0\)): {130, 155, 145}. Mean \(\bar{Y}_0 = 143.33\).

Our estimate is:
\[
\hat{\tau}_{ATE} = 140.0 - 143.33 = \mathbf{-3.33} \text{ mmHg}
\]
This estimate (-3.33) differs from the true ATE (-10.0) due to random sampling variability. Because our sample is tiny, this one particular randomization wasn’t perfectly balanced. However, the procedure is unbiased, meaning if we repeated this experiment many times, the average of our estimates would converge to the true value.
In our lab session, we will perform these calculations in R.
# Data from our example
df <- data.frame(
  sbp = c(130, 140, 150, 130, 155, 145),
  treatment = c(1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)
)

# 1. Manual difference-in-means
mean_treated <- mean(df$sbp[df$treatment == 1])
mean_control <- mean(df$sbp[df$treatment == 0])
ate_est <- mean_treated - mean_control
print(ate_est)
#> [1] -3.333333

# 2. Using a t-test (standard statistical procedure)
t.test(sbp ~ treatment, data = df, var.equal = TRUE)
# The output provides the means of both groups and the difference.

# 3. Using a linear model (regression)
model <- lm(sbp ~ treatment, data = df)
summary(model)
# The coefficient for 'treatment' is our ATE estimate!


❓ Check Your Understanding

Question: A study on a new tutoring program allows students to sign up voluntarily. Researchers find that tutored students have higher test scores. Why is this likely not a pure causal effect? What is the likely direction of the selection bias?


Answer

This is an observational study, not an RCT. Students who voluntarily sign up for tutoring are likely more motivated or have more parental support than those who do not. This means their baseline potential outcome, \(E[Y(0) | Z=1]\) (what their score would have been without tutoring), is likely higher than the baseline for the non-tutored group, \(E[Y(0) | Z=0]\). This is positive selection bias, which makes the tutoring program appear more effective than it truly is.



2. Question: In a study of a new fertilizer on corn fields, some fields are very large and some are small. The “treatment” is a uniform application rate (e.g., 10kg per hectare). Does this scenario potentially violate any part of SUTVA?


Answer

This could violate the Consistency assumption (“one version of the treatment”). While the application rate is the same, the actual farming practices, soil quality, and other factors might differ systematically between large and small fields. If the effect of the fertilizer depends on these other factors that are bundled with the unit type, one might argue there are different “versions” of how the treatment is experienced. There is no interference mentioned.

title: The Gold Standard: Randomized Experiments & Potential Outcomes
section: 📚 Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations and Theory
text:
📚 Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations and Theory

📕 Topic 1: Formal Proof of Unbiasedness of the ATE Estimator
Motivation: Proving that our estimator is “unbiased” is the theoretical guarantee that our estimation procedure, on average, will give us the right answer. It is the foundation for all valid inference in an RCT.
Derivation: We want to show that \(E[\hat{\tau}_{ATE}] = \text{ATE}\). The estimator is \(\hat{\tau}_{ATE} = \bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0\). By linearity of expectation, \(E[\hat{\tau}_{ATE}] = E[\bar{Y}_1] - E[\bar{Y}_0]\). Let’s analyze \(E[\bar{Y}_1] = E[Y_i | Z_i=1]\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
E[Y_i | Z_i=1] &= E[Z_i Y_i(1) + (1-Z_i)Y_i(0) | Z_i=1] & & \text{1. Substitute for } Y_i \
&= E[1 \cdot Y_i(1) + (1-1)Y_i(0) | Z_i=1] & & \text{2. Plug in } Z_i=1 \
&= E[Y_i(1) | Z_i=1] & & \text{3. Simplify} \
&= E[Y_i(1)] & & \text{4. By independence from randomization}
\end{aligned}
\]
Similarly, \(E[\bar{Y}_0] = E[Y_i | Z_i=0] = E[Y_i(0)]\). Therefore, \[
E[\hat{\tau}_{ATE}] = E[Y_i(1)] - E[Y_i(0)] = \text{ATE}
\]
The proof is complete. The key step (4) relies entirely on randomization making treatment assignment independent of potential outcomes.


📕 Topic 2: Variance of the ATE Estimator
Motivation: Unbiasedness tells us our aim is correct, but variance tells us about our precision. We need the variance to calculate standard errors and confidence intervals, which communicate the uncertainty in our estimate.
Derivation: The variance of our estimator is \(Var(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = Var(\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0)\). Because the treatment and control groups are independent samples, the variance of the difference is the sum of the variances:
\[
Var(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = Var(\bar{Y}_1) + Var(\bar{Y}_0)
\]
For the sample mean of the treated group, \(Var(\bar{Y}_1) = \frac{Var(Y_i | Z_i=1)}{n_1} = \frac{\sigma^2_1}{n_1}\). Similarly, \(Var(\bar{Y}_0) = \frac{\sigma^2_0}{n_0}\).
So, the true variance of the estimator is:
\[
Var(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = \frac{\sigma^2_1}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma^2_0}{n_0}
\]
In practice, we don’t know the true population variances \(\sigma^2_1\) and \(\sigma^2_0\). We estimate them using the sample variances from our data, \(S^2_1\) and \(S^2_0\). The estimated variance is: \[
\widehat{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = \frac{S^2_1}{n_1} + \frac{S^2_0}{n_0}
\]
The Standard Error (SE) is the square root of this estimated variance: \(SE(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = \sqrt{\frac{S^2_1}{n_1} + \frac{S^2_0}{n_0}}\).
✅ Worked Example:
From our observed data:

Treated Group {130, 140, 150}: \(n_1=3\), Sample Variance \(S^2_1 = \frac{(130-140)^2 + (140-140)^2 + (150-140)^2}{3-1} = 100\).
Control Group {130, 155, 145}: \(n_0=3\), Sample Variance \(S^2_0 = \frac{(130-143.33)^2 + (155-143.33)^2 + (145-143.33)^2}{3-1} \approx 175\).

\(\widehat{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = \frac{100}{3} + \frac{175}{3} \approx 33.33 + 58.33 = 91.66\)
\(SE(\hat{\tau}_{ATE}) = \sqrt{91.66} \approx \mathbf{9.57}\)


📕 Topic 3: Equivalence of Difference-in-Means and Simple Regression
Motivation: This proof provides a critical link between the simple, non-parametric approach of comparing means and the more flexible framework of linear regression. It shows that for the simplest case, they are identical, justifying our use of regression to estimate causal effects.
Derivation: Consider the simple linear regression model \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Z_i + \epsilon_i\), where \(Z_i \in {0, 1}\). The OLS estimator for \(\beta_1\) is \(\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{Cov(Z, Y)}{Var(Z)}\). Let \(p = n_1/N\) be the proportion treated.

Variance of Z: \(Var(Z) = E[Z^2] - (E[Z])^2 = p - p^2 = p(1-p)\).
Covariance of Z and Y: \(Cov(Z, Y) = E[ZY] - E[Z]E[Y]\).
\(E[ZY] = E[Y|Z=1]P(Z=1) + E[Y|Z=0]P(Z=0) = \bar{Y}_1 \cdot p + \bar{Y}_0 \cdot 0 = p\bar{Y}_1\).
\(E[Y] = \bar{Y}_1 \cdot p + \bar{Y}_0 \cdot (1-p)\).
\(Cov(Z, Y) = p\bar{Y}_1 - p(\bar{Y}_1 p + \bar{Y}_0 (1-p)) = p\bar{Y}_1 - p^2\bar{Y}_1 - p(1-p)\bar{Y}_0 = p(1-p)\bar{Y}_1 - p(1-p)\bar{Y}_0 = p(1-p)(\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0)\).

Now, we compute the ratio:
\[
\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{p(1-p)(\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0)}{p(1-p)} = \bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0
\]
This shows that the OLS estimate of the slope coefficient for a binary regressor is exactly the difference in the sample means between the group where \(Z=1\) and the group where \(Z=0\).

title: Week 4: The Potential Outcomes Framework
text:
So far, we have used Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) to visualize our causal assumptions. DAGs provide a “blueprint” for cause and effect. Now, we turn to the mathematical foundation that allows us to define and quantify what a “causal effect” actually is: the Potential Outcomes Framework, also known as the Rubin Causal Model.
At its core, every causal question is a “what if” question. What would have happened to a patient if they had received the new drug instead of the old one? What would the mortality rate be in a city if a clean-air policy had not been implemented? These questions require us to think about counterfactuals—outcomes that could have happened but didn’t. The Potential Outcomes framework provides the formal language to talk about these counterfactuals rigorously. It is the bedrock upon which most modern methods of causal inference are built.
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Define causal effects using the language of potential outcomes.
Explain the “Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference” and why we must shift our focus from individual to average effects.
Distinguish between different causal estimands: the ATE, ATT, and ATC.
Articulate and interpret the three key assumptions for identifying causal effects from data: Consistency, Positivity, and Exchangeability.
Decompose the simple difference in means into the causal effect and bias terms.

title: Week 4: The Potential Outcomes Framework
section: 1. Potential Outcomes and the Individual Causal Effect
text:
1. Potential Outcomes and the Individual Causal Effect
The Potential Outcomes framework starts with a simple but powerful idea. For any individual i and any given exposure or treatment A, there exists a set of potential outcomes, one for each possible treatment level.
For a binary treatment (A=1 for treated, A=0 for control):

\(Y_i(1)\): The potential outcome for individual i if they were to receive the treatment.
\(Y_i(0)\): The potential outcome for individual i if they were to receive the control.

Intuition: Imagine two parallel universes for a single patient with a headache. In Universe 1, they take an aspirin (\(A=1\)), and their headache level an hour later is \(Y_i(1)\). In Universe 2, they do not take an aspirin (\(A=0\)), and their headache level is \(Y_i(0)\).
Using this notation, we can define the individual causal effect (ICE) for person i as:
\[
\text{ICE}_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)
\]
This is the true, individual-level effect of the treatment.

3. Shifting Focus: Average Causal Effects
Since we cannot identify individual effects, causal inference shifts its goal to a more modest but achievable target: estimating the average causal effect for a population.
There are three primary average causal effects, or “estimands,” we often care about:

Average Treatment Effect (ATE):

\[
\text{ATE} = \E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]
\]
This is the average effect if everyone in the population were to be treated versus if everyone were to be in the control. It answers the question: “What is the effect of the treatment on a person chosen at random from the population?”

Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT):

\[
\text{ATT} = \E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) | A_i=1]
\]
This is the average effect specifically for the group of people who actually received the treatment. It answers the policy-relevant question: “How did the treatment affect the people who chose to receive it?”

Average Treatment Effect on the Controls (ATC or ATU):

\[
\text{ATC} = \E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) | A_i=0]
\]
This is the average effect specifically for the group of people who did not receive the treatment. It answers the question: “How would the treatment have affected the people who did not receive it?”
In a randomized controlled trial (RCT), the ATE, ATT, and ATC will all be the same. In observational studies, however, where individuals self-select into treatment, these estimands can be very different.

title: Week 4: The Potential Outcomes Framework
section: 4. The Three Key Assumptions for Identification
text:
4. The Three Key Assumptions for Identification
So, how do we use the data we actually observe to estimate these unobservable average causal effects? We need to make three critical assumptions that connect the potential outcomes to the observed data.






The Three Pillars of Causal Identification




Consistency: This assumption links the potential outcomes to the observed outcomes. It states that an individual’s observed outcome is their potential outcome under the treatment they actually received.

\[
\text{If } A_i = 1, \text{ then } Y_i = Y_i(1). \quad \text{If } A_i = 0, \text{ then } Y_i = Y_i(0).
\]
Intuition: This seems obvious, but it’s a crucial assumption. It means there is only one version of the treatment and that an individual’s outcome doesn’t depend on how they got assigned to the treatment, only on the treatment itself.

Positivity (or Overlap): For any set of characteristics, there is a non-zero probability of being in both the treatment and control groups.

\[
P(A=1 | Z=z) > 0 \text{ and } P(A=0 | Z=z) > 0 \text{ for all } z
\]
Intuition: You can’t learn about the effect of a drug on 80-year-olds if your study contains no 80-year-olds who took the drug. There must be overlap in the characteristics of the treated and control groups.

Exchangeability (or Ignorability / Unconfoundedness): This is the “no confounding” assumption. It states that the mechanism that assigns the treatment is independent of the potential outcomes.

Unconditional Exchangeability: \((Y(1), Y(0)) \indep A\)
Conditional Exchangeability: \((Y(1), Y(0)) \indep A | Z\)


Intuition: Unconditional exchangeability means the treated and control groups are, on average, identical with respect to all factors that could influence the outcome. This is what an RCT achieves through randomization. Conditional exchangeability is the assumption for observational studies: after adjusting for a set of measured covariates Z, the treated and control groups are “as-if” randomly assigned. This is the mathematical equivalent of satisfying the backdoor criterion in a DAG.

title: Week 4: The Potential Outcomes Framework
text:
✅ Theorem: Decomposing the Naive Difference
We can decompose the associational difference into two parts: the true causal effect and bias.
Derivation:
\[
\E[Y | A=1] - \E[Y | A=0]
\]
\[
= \E[Y(1) | A=1] - \E[Y(0) | A=0] \quad \text{(by Consistency)}
\]
Now, let’s add and subtract a clever term, \(\E[Y(0) | A=1]\):
\[
= \E[Y(1) | A=1] - \E[Y(0) | A=1] + \E[Y(0) | A=1] - \E[Y(0) | A=0]
\]
Grouping the terms:
\[
= \underbrace{\E[Y(1) - Y(0) | A=1]}_{\text{ATT}} + \underbrace{\{\E[Y(0) | A=1] - \E[Y(0) | A=0]\}}_{\text{Selection Bias}}
\]
Conclusion: The observed association is the sum of the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) and Selection Bias.

Selection Bias: This term represents the difference in the no-treatment potential outcome between the group that chose treatment and the group that chose control. If sicker people are more likely to take a drug, this term will be non-zero because the treated group would have had worse outcomes even without the drug.
Identification: The association equals the causal effect (ATT) if and only if the selection bias term is zero. This happens when \(\E[Y(0)|A=1] = \E[Y(0)|A=0]\), which is a direct implication of the exchangeability assumption.

title: Week 4: The Potential Outcomes Framework
text:
❓ Quiz: Check Your Understanding
You are evaluating a voluntary tutoring program (A=1) on students’ final exam scores (Y). You find that students in the program have lower average scores than those not in the program. An advisor argues this proves the program is ineffective.

What is the most likely form of bias at play here?
Using the potential outcomes framework, what key assumption is likely violated?
What is the ATT in this context, and what is the Selection Bias?



Answer


Selection Bias. Students who are struggling in the class are more likely to voluntarily sign up for tutoring.
Exchangeability is violated. The potential outcomes (exam scores with or without tutoring) are not independent of the decision to get tutoring. The treated group (tutored students) would have had lower scores than the control group even if no one had received tutoring.
The ATT is the true causal effect of the tutoring program for the struggling students who enrolled. It might be positive (e.g., +5 points). The Selection Bias is the difference in potential exam scores (without tutoring) between the struggling students who signed up and the proficient students who did not. This bias is likely large and negative (e.g., -15 points), overwhelming the positive ATT and making the observed association negative.

title: Week 4: The Potential Outcomes Framework
section: 📕 Motivation: How Randomization Guarantees an Unbiased Estimate
text:
📕 Motivation: How Randomization Guarantees an Unbiased Estimate
We’ve stated that in a randomized controlled trial (RCT), the simple difference in means is an unbiased estimator of the ATE. The potential outcomes framework allows us to prove this formally. This proof is the mathematical justification for the “gold standard” status of RCTs.

title: Week 4: The Potential Outcomes Framework
section: 📕 Derivation: Proof that the Naive Difference Identifies the ATE under Randomization
text:
📕 Derivation: Proof that the Naive Difference Identifies the ATE under Randomization
Goal: Show that under the assumptions of an ideal RCT, \(\E[Y | A=1] - \E[Y | A=0] = \E[Y(1) - Y(0)] = \text{ATE}\).
Assumptions of an Ideal RCT:

Consistency: Holds by ensuring a well-defined treatment protocol.
Positivity: Holds by design, as some units are assigned to treatment and some to control.
Unconditional Exchangeability: This is the key. Random assignment ensures that the treatment D is statistically independent of the pair of potential outcomes \((Y(1), Y(0))\).

\[
(Y(1), Y(0)) \indep A
\]
Step-by-step Derivation:

Start with the associational difference:

\[
\E[Y | A=1] - \E[Y | A=0]
\]

Apply the Consistency assumption:

\[
= \E[Y(1) | A=1] - \E[Y(0) | A=0]
\]

Apply the Unconditional Exchangeability assumption:

Because treatment assignment D is independent of the potential outcomes, conditioning on D provides no new information about the expected value of the potential outcomes.
Therefore, \(\E[Y(1) | A=1] = \E[Y(1)]\).
And, \(\E[Y(0) | A=0] = \E[Y(0)]\).
Annotation: This is the critical step. In an RCT, the group that got the treatment is, on average, a perfect mirror of the group that didn’t. Their average potential outcome under treatment would be the same as the population’s average.

Substitute back into the equation:

\[
= \E[Y(1)] - \E[Y(0)]
\]

Apply the definition of the ATE:

\[
= \E[Y(1) - Y(0)] = \text{ATE}
\]
Conclusion: This completes the proof. In a perfect RCT, the simple, observable difference in mean outcomes is a mathematically unbiased estimator of the unobservable Average Treatment Effect. This is why randomization is such a powerful tool for causal inference.

title: Week 1: What is a Causal Effect?
text:
Welcome to STAT 579! We begin our journey by tackling the most fundamental question of all: what exactly is a causal effect? It seems simple, but defining it with precision is the critical first step for every method we’ll learn.
Imagine you are a public health official. You observe that cities with higher numbers of public parks have lower rates of adult depression. Should you spend millions of dollars building new parks to improve mental health? Is the association causal, or could it be that healthier, wealthier people tend to live in cities that can afford more parks (confounding)? This is the kind of high-stakes question causal inference is designed to answer.
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Define a causal effect rigorously using the Potential Outcomes framework.
Explain the “Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference” as a missing data problem.
Articulate the crucial role of the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA).
Justify why Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) are a powerful tool for overcoming the fundamental problem.
Distinguish between association, causation, and confounding, and identify selection bias as the key obstacle in observational data.

title: Week 1: What is a Causal Effect?
text:
🔬 1. The Potential Outcomes Framework

Motivation & Intuition
To move from vague “what if” questions to formal analysis, we need a language to describe the unobserved. The Potential Outcomes Framework provides this language. The core idea is that for any treatment or exposure, there are multiple “potential worlds” that could occur for each individual.
Let’s consider a simple binary treatment, \(A\). For any individual \(i\), \(A_i=1\) if they receive the treatment and \(A_i=0\) if they receive the control. We imagine that for each individual, two potential outcomes exist simultaneously as fixed attributes, even before treatment is assigned.

\(Y_i^1\): The outcome for individual \(i\) if they were to be exposed to the treatment (\(A=1\)).
\(Y_i^0\): The outcome for individual \(i\) if they were to be exposed to the control (\(A=0\)).

These are also called counterfactuals because once a treatment is given, one of them will be counter-to-fact.

With this, we can define the Individual Causal Effect (ICE) for person \(i\) as:
\[
\tau_i = Y_i^1 - Y_i^0
\]

title: Week 1: What is a Causal Effect?
section: 💥 2. The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference
text:
💥 2. The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference

Motivation & Intuition
The core challenge of our field is that we can only live in one world at a time. Once a person receives a treatment, we can’t see what would have happened to them on the exact same day, at the exact same time, had they not received it. That alternate reality is lost to us.
For any individual, we can only ever observe one of their potential outcomes. The other is forever hidden. We can formalize this with a “switching equation” that links the potential outcomes to the single observed outcome, \(Y_i\):
\[
Y_i = A_i Y_i^1 + (1 - A_i) Y_i^0
\]
This means causal inference is fundamentally a missing data problem. Half the data in our ideal dataset is always missing.


🤔 Concept Check
A researcher measures a patient’s cholesterol, gives them a new drug for 6 months, and measures it again. The researcher claims the change in cholesterol is the causal effect. Why is this claim flawed according to the potential outcomes framework?
Answer: This “before-and-after” comparison is not a valid causal effect. The “before” measurement is not \(Y^0\). The potential outcome \(Y^0\) is what the patient’s cholesterol would have been after 6 months without the drug. Over 6 months, many other things could have changed (diet, exercise, aging), so the “before” value is not a valid counterfactual.

Since we can’t see the ICE, we aim for a more modest but achievable goal: estimating the Average Treatment Effect (ATE).
\[
\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}[Y^1 - Y^0]
\]
The ATE tells us the average effect of the treatment across an entire population.

title: Week 1: What is a Causal Effect?
section: ✨ 4. The Gold Standard: Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs)
text:
✨ 4. The Gold Standard: Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs)

Motivation & Intuition
How can we estimate the ATE if we are mortals and can’t see the full table? In an RCT, we randomly assign people to treatment or control. Randomization acts like a great equalizer: it ensures that, on average, the group that gets the treatment is no different from the group that doesn’t on all baseline characteristics. This property is called exchangeability.
Randomization makes the treatment assignment \(A\) statistically independent of the potential outcomes \({Y^1, Y^0}\):
\[
A \indep \{Y^1, Y^0\}
\]
Because of this, the mean of the observed outcomes in the treated group is a good estimate for the population mean of \(Y^1\), and likewise for the control group and \(Y^0\).
\[
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid A=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid A=0] = \mathbb{E}[Y^1] - \mathbb{E}[Y^0] = \text{ATE}
\]

title: Week 1: What is a Causal Effect?
section: 🚧 5. Observational Data & The Problem of Confounding
text:
🚧 5. Observational Data & The Problem of Confounding

Motivation & Intuition
Most of the time in public health, we can’t randomize. People choose their own exposures. This is observational data. In this setting, the treated and untreated groups are often not exchangeable. The reasons someone chooses a treatment might be linked to the outcome. This is called confounding. A confounder is a pre-treatment variable that is a common cause of both the treatment and the outcome.

When confounding exists, the simple difference in means is no longer the ATE. It is merely a measure of association, and it is biased.
\[
\text{Association} = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid A=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid A=0] \neq \text{ATE}
\]

section: 💡 6. SUTVA: The Rules of the Game
text:
💡 6. SUTVA: The Rules of the Game
All of this reasoning rests on a foundational assumption: the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA).






The Two Pillars of SUTVA




No Interference: One person’s treatment status does not affect another person’s outcome.

Violation Example: In a vaccine study, if my neighbor gets vaccinated, my chance of getting sick (\(Y_i^0\)) might decrease. My outcome is affected by their treatment.

Consistency: An individual’s observed outcome under their actual treatment is the same as their potential outcome under that treatment.

Violation Example: If the treatment is “exercise,” it’s ill-defined. One person might jog, another might lift weights. These are different versions of the treatment, each with its own potential outcome. Consistency requires a well-defined intervention.

title: Week 1: What is a Causal Effect?
text:
📚 Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations

Derivation: Decomposing Association into Causation and Bias
Motivation: Let’s formally prove why the associational difference was so wrong in our hand-calculated example. We can decompose it into the true causal effect and bias terms.
The associational difference is \(\Delta = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid A=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid A=0]\).
By consistency, we can write this as \(\Delta = \mathbb{E}[Y^1 \mid A=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y^0 \mid A=0]\).
Now, we add and subtract \(\mathbb{E}[Y^0 \mid A=1]\):
\[
\Delta = \underbrace{\left( \mathbb{E}[Y^1 \mid A=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y^0 \mid A=1] \right)}_{\text{Term 1: ATT}} + \underbrace{\left( \mathbb{E}[Y^0 \mid A=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y^0 \mid A=0] \right)}_{\text{Term 2: Selection Bias}}
\]

Term 1 is the Average Treatment effect on the Treated (ATT). A real causal effect, but only for the treated subgroup.
Term 2 is Selection Bias. It compares the baseline health (\(Y^0\)) of the treated group to the baseline health of the control group. If they’re different to start, this term is non-zero.



Hand-Calculated Example of the Decomposition
Let’s use our 10-person example to calculate these terms from the “divine” table.

Calculate ATT: We need the average causal effect just for the 5 people who got treated (Persons 3, 4, 7, 8, 10).


Their \(Y^1\) values are (6, 7, 8, 9, 10). Mean = 8.0.
Their \(Y^0\) values are (8, 9, 10, 11, 12). Mean = 10.0.
ATT = \(8.0 - 10.0 = -2.0\). (In this case, the effect is constant, so ATT = ATE).


Calculate Selection Bias: We compare the baseline health (\(Y^0\)) of the treated vs. the untreated.


The treated group’s \(Y^0\) values are (8, 9, 10, 11, 12). Mean \(\mathbb{E}[Y^0 \mid A=1] = 10.0\).
The untreated group’s \(Y^0\) values are (7, 6, 4, 5, 3). Mean \(\mathbb{E}[Y^0 \mid A=0] = 5.0\).
Selection Bias = \(10.0 - 5.0 = +5.0\).


Put it together: \[
\text{Association} = \text{ATT} + \text{Selection Bias}
\]

\[
+3.0 = -2.0 + 5.0
\]
This confirms our formula! Our observed association of +3.0 was a combination of the true causal effect of -2.0 and a large selection bias of +5.0 because the sicker group selected into treatment.

title: STAT 579: Applied Causal Inference
text:
Course Overview
This graduate-level seminar introduces the theory and application of causal inference, with a strong emphasis on biostatistical and epidemiological contexts. The course builds from conceptual foundations and core assumptions to modern estimation methods for causal effects, emphasizing target trial emulation as a unifying framework.
Key frameworks and tools include:

Potential Outcomes Framework & SUTVA
Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
Propensity Scores, IPW, and Doubly Robust Methods
Instrumental Variables
Mediation Analysis (NDE/NIE)
Marginal Structural Models (MSMs)
Sensitivity Analysis


Instructor’s Approach
Causal inference is not just a toolbox—it’s a rigorous way of thinking about cause and effect. We will prioritize:

Precise causal questions (not just statistical associations).
Transparency of assumptions (via DAGs and formal notation).
Identification before estimation (thinking carefully about what is learnable from data).
Critical robustness assessment (sensitivity, replication, target trial framing).

title: STAT 579: Applied Causal Inference

Learning Objectives
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

Formulate and distinguish causal from associational questions.
Represent assumptions using DAGs and counterfactual notation.
Evaluate and apply key assumptions (SUTVA, exchangeability, positivity).
Implement modern causal inference methods (propensity scores, IPW, MSMs, IVs, G-computation).
Decompose effects via mediation analysis.
Conduct sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding.
Frame observational studies as target trial emulations.
Critically evaluate causal claims in the literature.

title: Week 4: The Potential Outcomes Framework
text:
So far, we have used Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) to visualize our causal assumptions. DAGs provide a “blueprint” for cause and effect. Now, we turn to the mathematical foundation that allows us to define and quantify what a “causal effect” actually is: the Potential Outcomes Framework, also known as the Rubin Causal Model.
At its core, every causal question is a “what if” question. What would have happened to a patient if they had received the new drug instead of the old one? What would the mortality rate be in a city if a clean-air policy had not been implemented? These questions require us to think about counterfactuals—outcomes that could have happened but didn’t. The Potential Outcomes framework provides the formal language to talk about these counterfactuals rigorously. It is the bedrock upon which most modern methods of causal inference are built.
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Define causal effects using the language of potential outcomes.
Explain the “Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference” and why we must shift our focus from individual to average effects.
Distinguish between different causal estimands: the ATE, ATT, and ATC.
Articulate and interpret the three key assumptions for identifying causal effects from data: Consistency, Positivity, and Exchangeability.
Decompose the simple difference in means into the causal effect and bias terms.

section: Key Concepts: A Language for Counterfactuals
text:
Key Concepts: A Language for Counterfactuals

1. Potential Outcomes and the Individual Causal Effect
The Potential Outcomes framework starts with a simple but powerful idea. For any individual i and any given exposure or treatment D, there exists a set of potential outcomes, one for each possible treatment level.
For a binary treatment (D=1 for treated, D=0 for control):

\(Y_i(1)\): The potential outcome for individual i if they were to receive the treatment.
\(Y_i(0)\): The potential outcome for individual i if they were to receive the control.

Intuition: Imagine two parallel universes for a single patient with a headache. In Universe 1, they take an aspirin (\(D=1\)), and their headache level an hour later is \(Y_i(1)\). In Universe 2, they do not take an aspirin (\(D=0\)), and their headache level is \(Y_i(0)\).
Using this notation, we can define the individual causal effect (ICE) for person i as:
\[
\text{ICE}_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)
\]
This is the true, individual-level effect of the treatment.


2. The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference
The definition of the individual causal effect immediately reveals a profound challenge.






The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference



For any given individual i, it is impossible to observe both \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\) at the same time. We can only observe the outcome that corresponds to the treatment they actually received. The other potential outcome is a counterfactual and is forever missing.


We can represent this with a table. The question marks denote the unobserved, counterfactual outcomes.

Because we can never calculate \(Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\) for any single person, individual causal effects are fundamentally unobservable.


3. Shifting Focus: Average Causal Effects
Since we cannot identify individual effects, causal inference shifts its goal to a more modest but achievable target: estimating the average causal effect for a population.
There are three primary average causal effects, or “estimands,” we often care about:

Average Treatment Effect (ATE):

\[
\text{ATE} = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]
\]
This is the average effect if everyone in the population were to be treated versus if everyone were to be in the control. It answers the question: “What is the effect of the treatment on a person chosen at random from the population?”

Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT):

\[
\text{ATT} = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) | D_i=1]
\]
This is the average effect specifically for the group of people who actually received the treatment. It answers the policy-relevant question: “How did the treatment affect the people who chose to receive it?”

Average Treatment Effect on the Controls (ATC or ATU):

\[
\text{ATC} = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) | D_i=0]
\]
This is the average effect specifically for the group of people who did not receive the treatment. It answers the question: “How would the treatment have affected the people who did not receive it?”
In a randomized controlled trial (RCT), the ATE, ATT, and ATC will all be the same. In observational studies, however, where individuals self-select into treatment, these estimands can be very different.


4. The Three Key Assumptions for Identification
So, how do we use the data we actually observe to estimate these unobservable average causal effects? We need to make three critical assumptions that connect the potential outcomes to the observed data.






The Three Pillars of Causal Identification




Consistency: This assumption links the potential outcomes to the observed outcomes. It states that an individual’s observed outcome is their potential outcome under the treatment they actually received. \[
\text{If } D_i = 1, \text{ then } Y_i = Y_i(1). \quad \text{If } D_i = 0, \text{ then } Y_i = Y_i(0).
\]

Intuition: This seems obvious, but it’s a crucial assumption. It means there is only one version of the treatment and that an individual’s outcome doesn’t depend on how they got assigned to the treatment, only on the treatment itself.

Positivity (or Overlap): For any set of characteristics, there is a non-zero probability of being in both the treatment and control groups.

\[
P(D=1 | Z=z) > 0 \text{ and } P(D=0 | Z=z) > 0 \text{ for all } z
\]
Intuition: You can’t learn about the effect of a drug on 80-year-olds if your study contains no 80-year-olds who took the drug. There must be overlap in the characteristics of the treated and control groups.

Exchangeability (or Ignorability / Unconfoundedness): This is the “no confounding” assumption. It states that the mechanism that assigns the treatment is independent of the potential outcomes.

Unconditional Exchangeability: \((Y(1), Y(0)) \perp D\)
Conditional Exchangeability: \((Y(1), Y(0)) \perp D | Z\) Intuition: Unconditional exchangeability means the treated and control groups are, on average, identical with respect to all factors that could influence the outcome. This is what an RCT achieves through randomization. Conditional exchangeability is the assumption for observational studies: after adjusting for a set of measured covariates Z, the treated and control groups are “as-if” randomly assigned. This is the mathematical equivalent of satisfying the backdoor criterion in a DAG.

section: The Link Between Association and Causation
text:
The Link Between Association and Causation
Now we can use the potential outcomes framework to understand why “correlation is not causation.” The quantity we can always calculate from data is the association, or the simple difference in mean outcomes: \[
\text{Association} = E[Y | D=1] - E[Y | D=0]
\]
Is this equal to our causal estimand of interest, say, the ATE? Let’s see.

✅ Theorem: Decomposing the Naive Difference
We can decompose the associational difference into two parts: the true causal effect and bias.
Derivation: \[
E[Y | D=1] - E[Y | D=0]
\] \[
= E[Y(1) | D=1] - E[Y(0) | D=0] \quad \text{(by Consistency)}
\]
Now, let’s add and subtract a clever term, \(E[Y(0) | D=1]\): \[
= E[Y(1) | D=1] - E[Y(0) | D=1] + E[Y(0) | D=1] - E[Y(0) | D=0]
\]
Grouping the terms: \[
= \underbrace{E[Y(1) - Y(0) | D=1]}_{\text{ATT}} + \underbrace{\{E[Y(0) | D=1] - E[Y(0) | D=0]\}}_{\text{Selection Bias}}
\]
Conclusion: The observed association is the sum of the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) and Selection Bias.

Selection Bias: This term represents the difference in the no-treatment potential outcome between the group that chose treatment and the group that chose control. If sicker people are more likely to take a drug, this term will be non-zero because the treated group would have had worse outcomes even without the drug.
Identification: The association equals the causal effect (ATT) if and only if the selection bias term is zero. This happens when \(E[Y(0)|D=1] = E[Y(0)|D=0]\), which is a direct implication of the exchangeability assumption.

❓ Quiz: Check Your Understanding
You are evaluating a voluntary tutoring program (D=1) on students’ final exam scores (Y). You find that students in the program have lower average scores than those not in the program. An advisor argues this proves the program is ineffective.

What is the most likely form of bias at play here?
Using the potential outcomes framework, what key assumption is likely violated?
What is the ATT in this context, and what is the Selection Bias?



Answer


Selection Bias. Students who are struggling in the class are more likely to voluntarily sign up for tutoring.
Exchangeability is violated. The potential outcomes (exam scores with or without tutoring) are not independent of the decision to get tutoring. The treated group (tutored students) would have had lower scores than the control group even if no one had received tutoring.
The ATT is the true causal effect of the tutoring program for the struggling students who enrolled. It might be positive (e.g., +5 points). The Selection Bias is the difference in potential exam scores (without tutoring) between the struggling students who signed up and the proficient students who did not. This bias is likely large and negative (e.g., -15 points), overwhelming the positive ATT and making the observed association negative.

section: Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations and Theory
text:
Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations and Theory

📕 Motivation: How Randomization Guarantees an Unbiased Estimate
We’ve stated that in a randomized controlled trial (RCT), the simple difference in means is an unbiased estimator of the ATE. The potential outcomes framework allows us to prove this formally. This proof is the mathematical justification for the “gold standard” status of RCTs.


📕 Derivation: Proof that the Naive Difference Identifies the ATE under Randomization
Goal: Show that under the assumptions of an ideal RCT, \(E[Y | D=1] - E[Y | D=0] = E[Y(1) - Y(0)] = \text{ATE}\).
Assumptions of an Ideal RCT:

Consistency: Holds by ensuring a well-defined treatment protocol.
Positivity: Holds by design, as some units are assigned to treatment and some to control.
Unconditional Exchangeability: This is the key. Random assignment ensures that the treatment D is statistically independent of the pair of potential outcomes \((Y(1), Y(0))\). \[
(Y(1), Y(0)) \perp D
\]

Step-by-step Derivation:

Start with the associational difference: \[
E[Y | D=1] - E[Y | D=0]
\]
Apply the Consistency assumption: \[
= E[Y(1) | D=1] - E[Y(0) | D=0]
\]
Apply the Unconditional Exchangeability assumption:

Because treatment assignment D is independent of the potential outcomes, conditioning on D provides no new information about the expected value of the potential outcomes.
Therefore, \(E[Y(1) | D=1] = E[Y(1)]\).
And, \(E[Y(0) | D=0] = E[Y(0)]\).
Annotation: This is the critical step. In an RCT, the group that got the treatment is, on average, a perfect mirror of the group that didn’t. Their average potential outcome under treatment would be the same as the population’s average.

Substitute back into the equation:

\[
= E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)]
\]

Apply the definition of the ATE: \[
= E[Y(1) - Y(0)] = \text{ATE}
\]

Conclusion: This completes the proof. In a perfect RCT, the simple, observable difference in mean outcomes is a mathematically unbiased estimator of the unobservable Average Treatment Effect. This is why randomization is such a powerful tool for causal inference.

title: Week 4: The Potential Outcomes Framework
text:
The most widely accepted and clearest method is to use simple uppercase letters for observed variables and the same letters with parentheses for potential variables.


This is the most common and intuitive notation used in econometrics, epidemiology, and social sciences.


These represent the single reality that we see in our data for each individual. Use a simple, unadorned uppercase letter.

\(Y\): The observed outcome.
\(A\): The observed treatment status.
\(Z\): The observed instrument status.

For example, if we are studying a patient, \(Y\) is their actual measured health, and \(A\) is whether they actually took the drug.



These represent the hypothetical outcomes or states under different scenarios. Use the same uppercase letter followed by parentheses containing the specific condition.

\(Y(1)\): The potential outcome if the individual were to receive the treatment (\(A=1\)).
\(Y(0)\): The potential outcome if the individual were to not receive the treatment (\(A=0\)).
\(A(1)\): The potential treatment an individual would choose if exposed to the instrument (\(Z=1\)).

The power of this notation is that it makes the fundamental causal question explicit: we want to compare \(Y(1)\) and \(Y(0)\), but we can only ever observe one of them for any given person.




Another powerful framework, primarily from computer science and statistics, uses the do-operator to distinguish causation from association.

Association: The standard conditional expectation, \(E[Y|A=a]\), describes the average outcome among the subgroup of people who were observed to have treatment status \(a\). This is a simple statistical association.
Causation: The intervention-based expectation, \(E[Y|\text{do}(A=a)]\), describes the average outcome if we intervened and forced everyone in the population to take treatment \(a\).

These two systems are conceptually linked:
\[
E[Y(a)] = E[Y|\text{do}(A=a)]
\]
They represent the same causal quantity, just expressed in different notational languages.



For most applied work, the standard convention (\(Y\) vs. \(Y(a)\)) is recommended.

Clarity: It physically separates the observed world (\(Y\)) from the hypothetical world of potential outcomes (\(Y(a)\)) in a very intuitive way.
Explicitness: It makes the definition of causal effects, like the average treatment effect (\(E[Y(1) - Y(0)]\)), straightforward to write and understand.
Widespread Use: It’s the dominant notation in many fields, making your work more easily understood by a broader audience.

The key is consistency. Whichever system you choose, apply it consistently throughout your work to avoid ambiguity.

From Individuals to Populations
You’re also right that these concepts are like population values. While we can’t see a single person’s two potential outcomes, we can use statistical methods to estimate the average of these outcomes across a large group of people.

Individual Causal Effect (Unobservable): \(Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\)
Average Causal Effect (Estimable): \(E[Y(1) - Y(0)]\)

We treat the potential outcomes as the true, underlying parameters we want to learn about for a population.

title: Week 4: The Potential Outcomes Framework
text:
Comparison with do-calculus
Both potential outcomes and do-calculus are formal ways to talk about causation, but they use different metaphors.

Potential Outcomes (The “Two Worlds” Metaphor)
This framework, developed by Jerzy Neyman and Donald Rubin, asks you to imagine two parallel worlds:

A world where everyone receives the treatment (\(A=1\)). The average outcome here is \(E[Y(1)]\).
A world where no one receives the treatment (\(A=0\)). The average outcome here is \(E[Y(0)]\).

The causal effect is the difference in outcomes between these two hypothetical worlds.


do-calculus (The “Surgical Intervention” Metaphor)
This framework, developed by Judea Pearl, distinguishes between seeing and doing.

Seeing (Association): \(E[Y|A=1]\) is a passive observation. We look at the data and find the average outcome among people who happened to have received the treatment. This is just a correlation.

Example: Noticing that people who carry lighters have higher rates of cancer.

Doing (Causation): \(E[Y|\text{do}(A=1)]\) is an active intervention. We imagine performing “surgery” on the system, forcing everyone to receive the treatment and breaking any other factors that might have led them to choose it. This reveals the true causal effect.

Example: Estimating what would happen to cancer rates if we gave everyone a lighter. The rate wouldn’t change, revealing no causal link.




How They Relate
The two frameworks are logically equivalent. An intervention in the do-framework is the same as looking at the average outcome in one of the “potential outcome” worlds.
\[
E[Y(1)] = E[Y|\text{do}(A=1)]
\]
In short: Both systems provide a strict, mathematical language to ensure we’re estimating a real causal effect, not just a spurious correlation. The potential outcomes framework is often more intuitive for defining a causal question, while the do-calculus is especially powerful for determining if that question can be answered from a given dataset.
